newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends firm vs mark, yen but falls on stg in US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends firm vs mark, yen but falls on stg in US.

text.p: *Dlr/mark up but off highs over 1.73. *Dlr/yen holds firm.
*Trade thin pre-weekend G7, dollar overshadowed by early stg rise. *Cable near highs, strength vs mark a prop for dollar/mark.
*US/Japan pact to cooperate on Japan deregulation eases trade tension *Rubin, Mitsuzuka agreed excess currency volatility undesirable, seek close fx cooperation. Japan to push reform.
The dollar rose against the mark and yen but fell against the pound, which dominated trade and hit a 58-month high against the German mark on Friday.
"Sterling has been moving up quite nicely," said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston.
"Perhaps some fund managers are moving into it in anticipation of a rate hike, so there are some underlying investments moving that," he added.
The mark's weakness against the pound indirectly helped support the dollar against the German currency, while dollar/yen also made slow progress.

The pound extended overnight gains to 2.8645 marks in New York -- its highest level since August 1992 -- the start of a run on sterling that drove it out of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism the next month.
Against the dollar, the pound rose to $1.6555/65 from $1.6522/32 at the open.
But the dollar rose to 1.7285/90 marks from 1.7270/80 and to 114.80/90 yen, from 114.60/70.

Britain's new-Labor Party government inherited a robust economy and raised interest rates immediately after defeating the Conservative Party in May. The market believes Labor will deliver more rate hikes to catch up after months of foot-dragging by the previous government.
The pound was also helped by a report from the Confederation of British Industry showing increased orders for U.K exports.
Dollar/yen extended a three-day rally as friction over Japan's huge trade surplus ebbed while leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations gathered for a summit in Denver.
"People are starting to feel a little bit more comfortable on the whole trade issue with Japan," said David Solin, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto Thursday evening in Denver, was reported to have voiced concern about Japan's surplus, pointing to the damage to bilateral relations from surpluses in the past.
But Washington is discouraging dollar weakness, even though it might entice Japan to accept more U.S. exports.

Instead the administration is coaxing Japan to promote domestic-, rather than export-led growth, and said Thursday that Japan agreed to a formal consultative process to discuss deregulation of its economy.

"The way the U.S. is going to view that is as a kind of step in the right direction," Solin said. "If they feel Japan is moving in the right direction they don't want to come out and continue to bash them on trade."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka agreed on Friday that excess currency movements were undesirable, a Treasury spokesman said.
In other currency trading, the dollar rose to 1.4400/05 Swiss from 1.4388/98 and to Canadian $1.3885/90 from C$1.3878/83.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.7506/11 from $0.7489/94.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
